# Review of Last Class

## What Our LPs Assumed

- **Divisibility**: any fraction of a decision is allowed.
- Economic dispatch assumed every plant was **already on** and the only question was how much to generate.

**Raises the question**: how do we make decisions that are **discrete**, *e.g.* should a plant operate or not operate?

# Discrete Decisions

## Problems With Discrete Decisions

Some decisions can't be divided into fractions.

- Which generators to run this hour, not just how much?
- Whether to build a facility at all?
- How many trucks, pumps, or treatment units?

::: {.notes}
Economic dispatch took the set of running plants as given. In practice, operators also decide which plants to switch on, and a plant that's on has to produce at least its minimum and costs money just to keep running. Facility siting has the same structure: a site is either built or not.
:::

## Fixed Costs Cause Discontinuities

::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"}
units = 1:10
total_cost(x) = 3 + 2x                       # fixed cost 3, variable cost 2 per unit
p_fixed = plot(units, total_cost.(units), color=:black, marker=:circle, label="total cost",
    xlabel="Units of operation", ylabel="Cost", xticks=0:10, xlims=(-0.5, 10.5),
    ylims=(-0.5, 24), legend=:topleft, framestyle=:origin)
plot!(p_fixed, units, total_cost.(units) ./ units, color=cb_vermillion, linestyle=:dot,
    label="average cost per unit")
scatter!(p_fixed, [0], [0], color=:black, markersize=6)
plot!(p_fixed, size=(1200, 330), left_margin=10mm, bottom_margin=14mm)
```

A **fixed cost** to operate at all, plus a **variable cost** per unit, makes the cost jump at zero.

::: {.notes}
Operating costs nothing at zero output, then jumps to the fixed cost as soon as anything is produced. That jump can't be written as a linear function of output alone. The falling average cost (the dotted line) is an **economy of scale**: fixed costs favor fewer, larger operations.
:::

## Binary Variables

A **binary** (or **indicator**) variable is 1 if a condition is true and 0 if it is false:

$$u_g = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{false} \\ 1 & \text{true} \end{cases}$$

More generally, we also have **integer** variables: numbers of units, trucks, or turbines.

A linear program with some integer variables is a **mixed integer (linear) program** (MI(L)P).

::: {.notes}
Binary variables are integer variables restricted to 0 and 1. With them we can write fixed costs and on/off logic as linear expressions, at the price of losing divisibility.
:::

# Modeling With Binaries

## Which Plants Should Run?

``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"}
plants = ["Coal", "CCGT", "CT"]
min_output = [100, 50, 0]           # [MW] when on
max_output = [250, 200, 100]        # [MW]
marginal_cost = [20, 30, 50]        # [$/MWh]
fixed_cost = [3000, 1000, 100]      # [$/h] when on
println("| Plant | Minimum (MW) | Maximum (MW) | Marginal cost (\\\$/MWh) | Fixed cost when on (\\\$/h) |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for i in 1:3
    println("| $(plants[i]) | $(min_output[i]) | $(max_output[i]) | $(marginal_cost[i]) | $(commas(fixed_cost[i])) |")
end
```
| Plant | Minimum (MW) | Maximum (MW) | Marginal cost (\$/MWh) | Fixed cost when on (\$/h) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Coal | 100 | 250 | 20 | 3,000 |
| CCGT | 50 | 200 | 30 | 1,000 |
| CT | 0 | 100 | 50 | 100 |



Demand is **150 MW**. Which plants should run?

::: {.notes}
The merit-order instinct from dispatch says coal: it has the cheapest energy. But coal has the largest fixed cost, and its minimum output is 100 MW.
:::

## Linking Output to On/Off

**How can we write this with binaries $u_i$ and outputs $y_i$?**

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u}} \quad & \sum_i \left(\text{FixedCost}_i \, u_i + \text{MarginalCost}_i \, y_i\right) \\
\text{subject to:} \quad & \sum_i y_i \geq d \\[0.3em]
& y_i \leq P^{\text{max}}_i \, u_i \qquad \text{(no output when off)} \\[0.3em]
& y_i \geq P^{\text{min}}_i \, u_i \qquad \text{(at least the minimum when on)} \\[0.3em]
& u_i \in \{0, 1\}, \ y_i \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.notes}
Board item. The **linking constraint** multiplies the capacity by the binary. When u is 0, the plant's output is forced to zero; when u is 1, it can run between its minimum and maximum. The fixed cost is paid only when u is 1. The same pattern (capacity times a binary) switches facilities on and off in facility siting and network models.
:::

## The Three-Plant Model in `JuMP`

::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="false" code-line-numbers="|4,7,8|9-11|"}
function commit(demand; relax=false)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    @variable(model, y[1:3] >= 0)            # output [MW]
    @variable(model, u[1:3], Bin)            # on or off
    @objective(model, Min, sum(fixed_cost .* u) + sum(marginal_cost .* y))
    @constraint(model, sum(y) >= demand)
    @constraint(model, [i in 1:3], y[i] <= max_output[i] * u[i])
    @constraint(model, [i in 1:3], y[i] >= min_output[i] * u[i])
    if relax
        relax_integrality(model)             # drop integrality: an LP
    end
    set_silent(model)
    optimize!(model)
    return (output=value.(y), on=value.(u), cost=objective_value(model))
end
```
:::



::: {.notes}
`Bin` declares a binary variable. The rest is an ordinary LP model. The `relax` option is for later in the lecture.
:::

## Big-$M$ and Indicator Constraints

```julia
@variable(model, 0 <= y[i in 1:3] <= max_output[i])
@constraint(model, [i in 1:3], !u[i] => {y[i] <= 0})
@constraint(model, [i in 1:3], u[i] => {y[i] >= min_output[i]})
```

The linking constraints are **big-$M$ constraints**: a binary times a constant ($M = P^{\text{max}}_i$) switches a limit on or off. `JuMP` can also write them as **indicator constraints** (above). Some solvers don't accept these, so `JuMP` turns them into **big-$M$** constraints natively, but not all software does.

`JuMP` chooses $M$ using the largest `@variable` bounds; if any are unbounded it will throw an error.

::: {.notes}
For this model the indicator and big-$M$ versions give the same plans and costs at every demand in the lecture. Writing the big-$M$ constraints yourself works with any solver that handles binary variables, and lets you choose $M$. Bounds written as separate `@constraint`s don't count: `JuMP` needs them in `@variable`.
:::


## Logical Constraints

A water utility chooses new projects, with $u_j = 1$ if project $j$ is built:

::: {.small}
| Rule | Constraint |
|:--|:--|
| a reservoir at site 1 or site 2, not both | $u_1 + u_2 \leq 1$ |
| a treatment plant (3) only with a reservoir | $u_3 \leq u_1 + u_2$ |
| at least one new source: a reservoir or a well field (4) | $u_1 + u_2 + u_4 \geq 1$ |
:::

::: {.notes}
Each rule is a linear inequality on the binaries. To check one, list the combinations of the binaries it involves and confirm that the constraint allows exactly the combinations the rule allows: $u_3 \leq u_1 + u_2$ rules out only a treatment plant with no reservoir.
:::

# Branch and Bound

## Relaxing Integer Variables

The **LP relaxation** of a MILP is the same problem, but allowing integer variables to take fractional values.

**What do you think is the relationship between the solution to the LP relaxation and the solution of the original MILP?**

## Why the Relaxation Is a Bound

The integer points are a **subset** of the LP's region, so the relaxed optimum is:

- a **lower bound** when minimizing;
- an **upper bound** when maximizing.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The shaded region is an LP's feasible region; the dots are the integer points inside it. Dropping integrality can only add options, so the relaxed optimum is never worse than the integer optimum. For a minimization (like our plants) that makes it a lower bound on cost; for a maximization (the next example) an upper bound. In general the LP's corners are not integer points (network flow problems with integer supplies and capacities are an exception), so rounding the LP solution can give a point that is infeasible or far from optimal.
:::

## A Simple MILP

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & 3x_1 + 4x_2 \\
\text{subject to:} \quad & 2x_1 + 6x_2 \leq 27 \\
& x_2 \geq 2 \\
& 3x_1 + x_2 \leq 19 \\
& x_1, x_2 \geq 0, \ \text{integer}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Branch and bound**: solve LP relaxations, split on a fractional variable, and prune branches that can't beat the best integer solution found so far.

::: {.notes}
This example maximizes, so the relaxation gives an upper bound. Any integer point we find gives a lower bound. Branch and bound narrows the gap between them.
:::

## Node 1: The LP Relaxation

::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"}
# Solve the LP relaxation at a node, given extra bounds from branching
function node_lp(; x1_max=Inf, x1_min=0, x2_max=Inf, x2_min=2)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    @variable(model, x1_min <= x1 <= x1_max)
    @variable(model, x2_min <= x2 <= x2_max)
    @objective(model, Max, 3x1 + 4x2)
    @constraint(model, 2x1 + 6x2 <= 27)
    @constraint(model, 3x1 + x2 <= 19)
    set_silent(model)
    optimize!(model)
    if !is_solved_and_feasible(model)
        return nothing                       # the node is infeasible
    end
    return (x1=value(x1), x2=value(x2), z=objective_value(model))
end

# Draw the region allowed at a node, its integer points, and its LP optimum
function node_plot(; x1_max=Inf, x1_min=0, x2_max=Inf, x2_min=2, title="")
    p = plot(xlabel=L"x_1", ylabel=L"x_2", xlims=(0, 6), ylims=(0, 5), framestyle=:origin,
        xticks=0:6, yticks=0:5, title=title)
    # shade the region allowed at this node
    xs = range(max(0, x1_min), min(6, x1_max); length=200)
    top_edge = zeros(length(xs))
    for k in eachindex(xs)
        top_edge[k] = min((27 - 2xs[k]) / 6, 19 - 3xs[k], x2_max)
    end
    inside = top_edge .>= x2_min
    if any(inside)
        plot!(p, xs[inside], fill(x2_min, count(inside)), fillrange=top_edge[inside],
            color=cb_sky, alpha=0.5, linewidth=0)
    end
    plot!(p, 0:0.1:6, (27 .- 2 .* (0:0.1:6)) ./ 6, color=cb_purple)
    plot!(p, 0:0.1:6, 19 .- 3 .* (0:0.1:6), color=cb_blue, linestyle=:dash)
    hline!(p, [2], color=cb_vermillion, linestyle=:dashdot)
    # mark the integer points allowed at this node
    for i in 0:6
        for j in 2:5
            if 2i + 6j <= 27 && 3i + j <= 19 && x1_min <= i <= x1_max && x2_min <= j <= x2_max
                scatter!(p, [i], [j], color=:black, markersize=6)
            end
        end
    end
    sol = node_lp(x1_max=x1_max, x1_min=x1_min, x2_max=x2_max, x2_min=x2_min)
    if !isnothing(sol)
        scatter!(p, [sol.x1], [sol.x2], color=cb_yellow, markersize=11,
            markerstrokecolor=:black, markerstrokewidth=2)
    end
    return p, sol
end

# Objective values to two places, with no decimals on whole numbers
function show_z(z)
    z_two_places = round(z; digits=2)
    if isinteger(z_two_places)
        return string(round(Int, z_two_places))
    end
    return string(z_two_places)
end

# A node's objective, or "infeasible"
function show_node(sol)
    if isnothing(sol)
        return "infeasible"
    end
    return show_z(sol.z)
end

# Every node of the tree, in the order it is solved
tree_nodes = [node_lp(),
    node_lp(x2_max=2), node_lp(x2_min=3),
    node_lp(x2_min=3, x1_max=4), node_lp(x2_min=3, x1_min=5),
    node_lp(x2_max=2, x1_max=5), node_lp(x2_max=2, x1_min=6),
    node_lp(x2_min=3, x2_max=3, x1_max=4), node_lp(x2_min=4, x1_max=4)]
parent = [0, 1, 1, 3, 3, 2, 2, 4, 4]              # the node each one branched from
branch = ["", L"x_2 \leq 2", L"x_2 \geq 3", L"x_1 \leq 4", L"x_1 \geq 5",
    L"x_1 \leq 5", L"x_1 \geq 6", L"x_2 \leq 3", L"x_2 \geq 4"]
node_x = [0, -2, 2, 1, 3, -3, -1, 0, 2]           # where each node is drawn
node_y = [4.1, 2.8, 2.8, 1.5, 1.5, 1.5, 1.5, 0.2, 0.2]
half_width = 0.9
half_height = 0.43

# Is a node's LP solution integer?
function is_integer_node(sol)
    if isnothing(sol)
        return false
    end
    return abs(sol.x1 - round(sol.x1)) < 1e-6 && abs(sol.x2 - round(sol.x2)) < 1e-6
end

# After the first n_solved nodes: the lower bound (the best integer solution so far,
# starting from the rounded point of node 1) and the upper bound (the best LP value
# among the nodes not branched yet), with the nodes they come from (0 for rounding)
function bounds_after(n_solved)
    lower = rounded_z
    lower_node = 0
    for k in 1:n_solved
        if is_integer_node(tree_nodes[k]) && tree_nodes[k].z >= lower - 1e-9
            lower = tree_nodes[k].z
            lower_node = k
        end
    end
    upper = -Inf
    upper_node = 0
    for k in 1:n_solved
        has_child = false
        for j in 2:n_solved
            if parent[j] == k
                has_child = true
            end
        end
        if !has_child && !isnothing(tree_nodes[k]) && tree_nodes[k].z > upper
            upper = tree_nodes[k].z
            upper_node = k
        end
    end
    return (lower=lower, lower_node=lower_node, upper=upper, upper_node=upper_node)
end

# Draw node k's box: dashed if it is still to be solved
function node_box!(p, k, fill_color; dashed=false)
    box_x = node_x[k] .+ [-half_width, half_width, half_width, -half_width]
    box_y = node_y[k] .+ [-half_height, -half_height, half_height, half_height]
    if dashed
        plot!(p, Shape(box_x, box_y), fillcolor=fill_color, linecolor=:black,
            linewidth=1.5, linestyle=:dash)
    else
        plot!(p, Shape(box_x, box_y), fillcolor=fill_color, fillalpha=0.35,
            linecolor=:black, linewidth=1.5)
    end
    return p
end

# The tree after the first n_solved nodes, with the next `pending` nodes drawn empty
function tree_plot(n_solved; pending=0)
    bounds = bounds_after(n_solved)
    lower = bounds.lower
    p = plot(xlims=(-4, 4), ylims=(-0.25, 4.55), framestyle=:none, ticks=nothing,
        size=(1200, 350), left_margin=0mm, bottom_margin=0mm)
    # the bounds so far, in the top left corner
    if bounds.lower_node == 0
        lower_source = "rounding"
    else
        lower_source = "node $(bounds.lower_node)"
    end
    annotate!(p, -3.95, 4.3, text("Upper bound: $(show_z(bounds.upper)) (node $(bounds.upper_node))",
        18, :left, plot_font))
    annotate!(p, -3.95, 3.9, text("Lower bound: $(show_z(lower)) ($(lower_source))", 18, :left,
        plot_font))
    # each branch, labelled at its midpoint with the bound it adds; a white patch
    # breaks the line behind the label
    for k in 2:(n_solved + pending)
        j = parent[k]
        plot!(p, [node_x[j], node_x[k]], [node_y[j] - half_height, node_y[k] + half_height],
            color=:gray40, linewidth=2)
        mid_x = (node_x[j] + node_x[k]) / 2
        mid_y = (node_y[j] + node_y[k]) / 2
        plot!(p, Shape(mid_x .+ [-0.3, 0.3, 0.3, -0.3], mid_y .+ [-0.15, -0.15, 0.15, 0.15]),
            fillcolor=:white, linecolor=:white, linewidth=0)
        annotate!(p, mid_x, mid_y, text(branch[k], 17, :center))
    end
    # solved nodes: green for an integer solution, gray where a branch ends without one
    for k in 1:n_solved
        sol = tree_nodes[k]
        box_color = :white
        if isnothing(sol)
            top_line = "Node $(k)"
            bottom_line = "infeasible"
            box_color = :gray70
        else
            top_line = "Node $(k): Z = $(show_z(sol.z))"
            bottom_line = "($(show_z(sol.x1)), $(show_z(sol.x2)))"
            if is_integer_node(sol)
                status = "integer"
                if n_solved == length(tree_nodes) && abs(sol.z - lower) < 1e-9
                    status = "optimum"
                end
                bottom_line = bottom_line * ", " * status
                box_color = cb_green
            elseif sol.z < lower - 1e-9
                bottom_line = bottom_line * ", pruned"
                box_color = :gray70
            end
        end
        node_box!(p, k, box_color)
        annotate!(p, node_x[k], node_y[k] + 0.18, text(top_line, 18, plot_font))
        annotate!(p, node_x[k], node_y[k] - 0.18, text(bottom_line, 18, plot_font))
    end
    # nodes still to solve
    for k in (n_solved + 1):(n_solved + pending)
        node_box!(p, k, :white; dashed=true)
        annotate!(p, node_x[k], node_y[k], text("Node $(k)", 18, plot_font))
    end
    return p
end

p1, node1 = node_plot()
rounded = (floor(Int, node1.x1), floor(Int, node1.x2))    # round the LP point down
rounded_z = 3 * rounded[1] + 4 * rounded[2]

# The walkthrough's claims: the order of branching, which nodes are infeasible or
# integer, and where the bounds meet
@assert bounds_after(3).upper_node == 3 && bounds_after(5).upper_node == 2
@assert bounds_after(7).upper_node == 4
@assert isnothing(tree_nodes[5]) && isnothing(tree_nodes[7])
@assert is_integer_node(tree_nodes[6]) && is_integer_node(tree_nodes[8])
@assert abs(tree_nodes[6].z - rounded_z) < 1e-9 && tree_nodes[9].z < tree_nodes[8].z
@assert abs(bounds_after(9).upper - bounds_after(9).lower) < 1e-9

plot!(p1, size=(1100, 300), left_margin=8mm)
```

:::



No integer lies strictly between 2 and 3, so every integer solution is in node 2 ($x_2 \leq 2$) or node 3 ($x_2 \geq 3$).

::: {.notes}
Each branch adds one bound to node 1's LP, and each new node is an LP to solve.
:::

## The LPs at Nodes 2 and 3

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & 3x_1 + 4x_2 \\
\text{subject to:} \quad & 2x_1 + 6x_2 \leq 27 \\
& x_2 \geq 2 \\
& 3x_1 + x_2 \leq 19 \\
& x_1, x_2 \geq 0 \\
& x_2 \leq 2 \quad (\text{node } 2) \qquad \text{or} \qquad x_2 \geq 3 \quad (\text{node } 3)
\end{aligned}
$$

Neither LP requires integer values: integrality enters only through the bounds added by branching.

::: {.notes}
Board item. Shade the strip $2 < x_2 < 3$ on node 1's plot: branching removes it, and it holds no integer points.
:::

## Solving Nodes 2 and 3

::: {#22 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"}

p3, node3 = node_plot(x2_min=3, title=L"x_2 \geq 3")
plot(p2, p3, layout=(1, 2), size=(1100, 320), left_margin=8mm)
```

The upper and lower bounds meet at **24**: the optimum is (4, 3).

::: {.notes}
Green boxes are integer solutions; gray boxes end a branch. A branch ends when its node is infeasible, when its solution is integer (nothing below can do better), or when its value is below the lower bound. In the worst case the tree grows exponentially with the number of integer variables, which is why MILP solvers, HiGHS included, add cutting planes and heuristics (branch and cut).
:::

# Key Takeaways and Upcoming Schedule

## Key Takeaways

::: {.incremental}
- **Binary variables** turn on/off decisions into linear constraints: fixed cost × $u$, output ≤ capacity × $u$.
- The **LP relaxation** bounds the MILP (below for min, above for max), but its solution can have fractional values for the binaries, such as a plant that is partly on.
- **Branch and bound** solves relaxations, branches on fractional variables, and prunes.
:::
